claims.text: The construction industry remains one of the least automated sectors.
claims.poster_quote: The construction industry remains one of the least automated sectors, despite its economic scale and high-risk tasks—especially on roofs.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The construction industry is among the least automated sectors with respect to robotics, despite its substantial economic relevance [6].
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the construction industry is among the least automated sectors.

claims.text: Roof work involves hazardous conditions like falls and repetitive physical labor.
claims.poster_quote: Roof work involves hazardous conditions like falls and repetitive physical labor, making it ideal for robotic automation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Within this domain, work on roofs represents a particularly hazardous area. Tasks such as construction, maintenance, installation, and inspection expose workers to significant risks, with slipping and falling accidents constituting a major cause of fatalities [7]. At the same time, many tasks on roofs are physically demanding and repetitive, providing a strong motivation to explore robotic assistance.
claims.reason: The paper states that roof work involves hazardous conditions like slipping and falling, and tasks are physically demanding and repetitive.

claims.text: Quadruped robots remain underutilized in real-world applications.
claims.poster_quote: Quadruped robots, while increasingly capable, remain underutilized in real-world applications.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Although these tasks have been proposed for a long time and quadruped capabilities have rapidly advanced, commercialization and deployment in these applications remain limited.
claims.reason: The paper notes that commercialization and deployment of quadruped robots remain limited.

claims.text: This work investigates whether commercial quadrupeds like the Unitree Go2 can operate effectively on tiled roofs.
claims.poster_quote: This work investigates whether commercial quadrupeds like the Unitree Go2 can operate effectively on tiled roofs—a novel, unexplored environment combining steep inclines, smooth surfaces, and discrete structural features.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A dedicated test rig of a roof’s surface was designed to evaluate the baseline performance of a commercial quadruped, the Unitree Go2, in this new environment.
claims.reason: The paper describes using a dedicated test rig to evaluate the baseline performance of the Unitree Go2 in a roof environment.

claims.text: A custom test rig simulating a German-style tiled roof (Frankfurther Pfanne) was built to evaluate the Unitree Go2’s performance.
claims.poster_quote: A custom test rig simulating a German-style tiled roof (Frankfurther Pfanne) was built to evaluate the Unitree Go2’s performance.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To objectively assess the performance of the Go2 (software version 1.4.4) and create a baseline for future comparison with custom feet, an adjustable test rig of a roof environment was developed (see Fig. 1). As surface material the Frankfurther Pfanne was chosen, which is the most common type of roof tile in Germany [2].
claims.reason: The paper confirms that an adjustable test rig using the Frankfurther Pfanne (the most common German roof tile) was developed to assess the Go2.

claims.text: Three core locomotion tasks were tested: balancing on increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences in multiple orientations, and incline walking.
claims.poster_quote: Three core locomotion tasks were tested: balancing on increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences in multiple orientations, and incline walking.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: With the Go2, three core skills were examined: balancing on continuously increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences, and incline walking.
claims.reason: The paper lists these three core skills as the focus of the experiments.

claims.text: Motion capture (OptiTrack) tracked foot slippage via reflective markers.
claims.poster_quote: Motion capture (OptiTrack) tracked foot slippage via reflective markers.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Incline walking was evaluated by repeatedly ascending increasingly higher slopes while measuring slippage using the OptiTrack system to track reflective markers positioned at the sides of the ball feet.
claims.reason: The paper states that the OptiTrack motion capture system was used to track reflective markers on the feet to measure slippage.

claims.text: Friction coefficients were measured using a UR10e force-torque sensor.
claims.poster_quote: Friction coefficients were measured using a UR10e force-torque sensor.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: As a preliminary experiment the dynamic coefficient of friction f of the ball feet was measured by using the internal force-torque sensor of a UR10e.
claims.reason: The paper states that the dynamic coefficient of friction was measured using the internal force-torque sensor of a UR10e.

claims.text: All trials were automated via Python using WebRTC.
claims.poster_quote: All trials were automated via Python using WebRTC, with the robot set to standard walking mode at 1.0 m/s.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For high repeatability reasons, all trials were controlled via Python using the WebRTC implementation provided by Severov [16].
claims.reason: The paper states that all trials were controlled via Python using WebRTC.

claims.text: The robot was set to standard walking mode at 1.0 m/s.
claims.poster_quote: All trials were automated via Python using WebRTC, with the robot set to standard walking mode at 1.0 m/s.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The robot was set to standard walking mode and a target speed of 1.0 m s−1.
claims.reason: The paper confirms the robot was set to standard walking mode at a target speed of 1.0 m/s.

claims.text: Experiments were repeated 10 times per condition.
claims.poster_quote: Experiments were repeated 10 times per condition for statistical significance.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To create statistical significance every experiment is repeated ten times.
claims.reason: The paper states that every experiment was repeated ten times.

claims.text: Friction alone cannot predict locomotion success.
claims.poster_quote: Friction alone cannot predict locomotion success—dynamic load redistribution and control matter more.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Dynamic locomotion performance cannot be predicted from friction measurements alone.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that dynamic locomotion performance cannot be predicted from friction measurements alone.

claims.text: Center-of-mass shifts toward rear legs on inclines reduce front-foot friction.
claims.poster_quote: Center-of-mass shifts toward rear legs on inclines reduce front-foot friction, requiring incline-aware control.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: As incline angle increases, the center of mass shifts toward the rear legs, reducing normal forces and therefore friction forces at the front feet.
claims.reason: The paper explains that the center of mass shifts toward the rear legs on inclines, reducing normal and friction forces at the front feet.

claims.text: Discrete terrain features (tile steps, curves) dominate slip events.
claims.poster_quote: Discrete terrain features (tile steps, curves) dominate slip events, demanding perception and precise foothold selection.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Slippage was frequently triggered by abrupt slip-off events at tile steps and curved sections, even on 0◦ incline. This suggests that roof locomotion is governed by discrete terrain interactions rather than purely planar slope mechanics.
claims.reason: The paper states that slippage was frequently triggered by discrete terrain features like tile steps and curved sections.

claims.text: Standard controllers apply uniform push-off forces, exceeding friction cones on slopes.
claims.poster_quote: Standard controllers apply uniform push-off forces, exceeding friction cones on slopes—adaptive gait parameters are essential.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The evaluated controller applied similar push-off forces and gait timing across all inclines. This resulted in tangential forces exceeding the friction cone on steeper slopes.
claims.reason: The paper states that the controller applied similar push-off forces across all inclines, causing tangential forces to exceed the friction cone.

claims.text: Ball feet have a small contact area and lack terrain adaptation.
claims.poster_quote: Ball feet’s small contact area and lack of terrain adaptation are critical hardware limitations; future designs need larger, high-friction, interlocking surfaces.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Ball-shaped feet exhibited systematic limitations due to their small contact area and lack of geometric adaptation to tiled surfaces.
claims.reason: The paper notes that ball-shaped feet have a small contact area and lack geometric adaptation.

claims.text: Get-up/lie-down motions must be terrain-aware or restricted to level surfaces.
claims.poster_quote: Get-up/lie-down motions must be terrain-aware or restricted to level surfaces.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Safe deployment therefore requires incline-aware recovery behaviors or dedicated level activation areas.
claims.reason: The paper states that safe deployment requires incline-aware recovery behaviors (terrain-aware) or dedicated level activation areas.

claims.text: The Go2 failed to meet manufacturer claims of 40° slope capability.
claims.poster_quote: The Go2 failed to meet manufacturer claims of 40° slope capability.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Manufacturer claims of slopeclimbing capabilities of up to 40◦ were not achieved under the test conditions [18].
claims.reason: The paper confirms that manufacturer claims of up to 40° slope-climbing capabilities were not achieved.

claims.text: Standing balance failed at 27.58° ± 0.72°.
claims.poster_quote: Standing balance failed at 27.58° ± 0.72°, primarily due to front-limb slippage.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For standing on an incline, the critical angle was measured at (27.58 ± 0.72)◦ on average.
claims.reason: The paper states that the critical angle for standing on an incline was 27.58° ± 0.72°.

claims.text: Standing balance failure was primarily due to front-limb slippage.
claims.poster_quote: Standing balance failed at 27.58° ± 0.72°, primarily due to front-limb slippage.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Failures during balancing were consistently preceded by slippage of the front limbs.
claims.reason: The paper states that balancing failures were consistently preceded by slippage of the front limbs.

claims.text: Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11° (head-up/down).
claims.poster_quote: Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11° (head-up/down) and 7° (sideways), failing when the center of mass exited the support polygon.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Full task success was achieved only at low inclines: up to 11.0◦ for head-up and head-down orientations, and up to 7.0◦ for the sideways orientation.
claims.reason: The paper states that get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11.0° for head-up and head-down orientations.

claims.text: Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 7° (sideways).
claims.poster_quote: Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11° (head-up/down) and 7° (sideways), failing when the center of mass exited the support polygon.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Full task success was achieved only at low inclines: up to 11.0◦ for head-up and head-down orientations, and up to 7.0◦ for the sideways orientation.
claims.reason: The paper states that get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 7.0° for the sideways orientation.

claims.text: Get-up/lie-down failed when the center of mass exited the support polygon.
claims.poster_quote: Get-up/lie-down succeeded only up to 11° (head-up/down) and 7° (sideways), failing when the center of mass exited the support polygon.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In all cases, failures occurred when the center of mass (COM) exited the support polygon during the pre-programmed motion.
claims.reason: The paper states that failures occurred when the center of mass exited the support polygon.

claims.text: Incline walking showed a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001).
claims.poster_quote: Incline walking showed a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001), with critical failures occurring regularly at 25°.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Regression analysis revealed ... a highly significant (p(F ) < 0.001) quadratic relationship between incline angle and slippage...
claims.reason: The paper confirms a highly significant quadratic relationship (p(F) < 0.001) between incline angle and slippage.

claims.text: Critical failures occurred regularly at 25° during incline walking.
claims.poster_quote: Incline walking showed a quadratic increase in slippage with incline angle (p < 0.001), with critical failures occurring regularly at 25°.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Experiments revealed that standard ball feet are inherently inadequate for locomotion on sloped roofs: slippage increased quadratically with incline angle, get-up and lie-down sequences were only possible on small inclines, and critical failures already occurred regularly on moderate inclines of 25◦.
claims.reason: The paper states that critical failures occurred regularly on moderate inclines of 25°.

claims.text: Even on flat ground, tile steps caused slippage.
claims.poster_quote: Even on flat ground, tile steps caused slippage.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The X -direction plots also show that the roof environment makes the robot slip even on flat ground, due to the small steps between individual rows of tiles.
claims.reason: The paper states that the robot slips even on flat ground due to the small steps between rows of tiles.

claims.text: Regression analysis confirmed a linear decrease in traveled distance.
claims.poster_quote: Regression analysis confirmed a linear decrease in traveled distance and no significant correlation with trajectory deviation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Regression analysis revealed a highly significant (p < 0.0035) linear relationship between incline angle and traveled distance...
claims.reason: The paper confirms a highly significant linear relationship between incline angle and traveled distance, which Table 2 shows is negative (decreasing).

claims.text: Regression analysis showed no significant correlation with trajectory deviation.
claims.poster_quote: Regression analysis confirmed a linear decrease in traveled distance and no significant correlation with trajectory deviation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Regression analysis revealed ... no explainable correlation between incline angle and trajectory deviation.
claims.reason: The paper states that there was no explainable correlation between incline angle and trajectory deviation.

claims.text: Friction coefficients were 1.144 (flat).

claims.paper_evidence: The coefficient of friction for a rubber ball foot on a roof tile was measured at 1.144 ± 0.1299 on flat and 1.430 ± 0.1298 on curved sections of the roof.
claims.reason: The paper states that the coefficient of friction on flat sections was 1.144 ± 0.1299.

claims.text: Friction coefficients were 1.430 (curved).
claims.poster_quote: Friction coefficients were 1.144 (flat) and 1.430 (curved), suggesting theoretical inclines >48°, but dynamic performance fell far short—highlighting control and stability as key bottlenecks.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The coefficient of friction for a rubber ball foot on a roof tile was measured at 1.144 ± 0.1299 on flat and 1.430 ± 0.1298 on curved sections of the roof.
claims.reason: The paper states that the coefficient of friction on curved sections was 1.430 ± 0.1298.

claims.text: Friction coefficients suggest theoretical inclines >48°.
claims.poster_quote: Friction coefficients were 1.144 (flat) and 1.430 (curved), suggesting theoretical inclines >48°, but dynamic performance fell far short—highlighting control and stability as key bottlenecks.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Using Eq. (1), this leads to respective maximum material specific incline angles ρ of (48.84 ± 3.22)◦ and (55.03 ± 2.44)◦.
